# Trees

This third part of the Codex is where the data structures stop being *flat*. Parts I and II lived on sequences and partitions; nothing in either had a parent or a depth. The eight chapters in this part introduce **hierarchical** data structures — every element has a parent (sometimes one, sometimes implicit), and the cost shape of every operation becomes some function of the tree's height. For a balanced tree of $n$ nodes, that's $\Theta(\log n)$ — the missing middle between Part I's $\Theta(n)$ and Part II's $\Theta(1)$, and the right cost for most workloads where sorted data has to change.

The arc of the part is a progression in how the tree's shape gets maintained.

* **Binary trees** (chapter 15) lay down the substrate — the four traversals (pre-, in-, post-, level-order), Morris's no-stack threaded walk, and pre-order-with-nulls serialization. No ordering constraint yet — just a recursive type definition and the recursion that walks it.
* **Binary search trees** (chapter 16) add a single ordering rule (smaller on the left, bigger on the right). The in-order traversal of a BST is sorted — that's the entire structure restated. Insert, search, and the three-case delete all become $\Theta(h)$, where $h$ is the tree's height. And then the sorted-input pathology shows what can go wrong.
* **Self-balancing BSTs** (chapter 17) fix the height. AVL trees enforce $|h_\text{left} - h_\text{right}| \le 1$ at every node and repair violations with constant-time rotations on the way back up the recursion. The Fibonacci-tree argument gives $h \le 1.44 \log_2 n$. A sidebar names why production picks red-black trees instead.
* **Treaps** (chapter 18) get the same balance probabilistically. Each node carries a random priority; the structure maintains BST order on keys and max-heap order on priorities; the expected height is $O(\log n)$ inherited from the random-permutation analysis of chapter 16. A first taste of randomization-as-balance, which returns in Part IX.
* **Heaps and priority queues** (chapter 19) drop the BST property and keep only the heap order. The whole tree lives in an array via index arithmetic: parent at $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$, children at $2i+1$ and $2i+2$. Build-heap in $\Theta(n)$ via Floyd's bottom-up trick — the implicit-tree-as-array pattern returns in chapters 21 and 22.
* **Tries** (chapter 20) make the tree's *path* encode the key. One node per character, a `terminal` flag for stored words, and the prefix queries hash tables physically can't answer. Compressed (radix) tries collapse single-child chains, and longest-prefix matching turns the structure into an IP-routing engine.
* **Segment trees** (chapter 21) take the array-as-implicit-tree pattern from heaps and apply it to range queries. Every node owns an interval; the answer to a range query is the sum of the $O(\log n)$ canonical intervals that tile it. Lazy propagation pushes the structure to $O(\log n)$ on both range update and range query.
* **Fenwick trees** (chapter 22) are the same problem at half the code. For invertible monoids — sum, xor, count — the `i & -i` lowest-set-bit trick gives you point update + prefix query in eight lines per operation. The trade against segment trees: shorter code, restricted to aggregates with inverses.

By the end of this part you'll be fluent in eight tree-shaped structures and four moves that come back through the rest of the book: **rotations** as the universal repair operation for ordered trees (chapters 17, 18), **the implicit-array-as-tree pattern** (chapters 19, 21, 22) where the tree's shape lives in index arithmetic and saves you a node-per-element allocation, **path-encodes-key** (chapter 20) where the structural position *is* the data, and **balance as invariant** in either its deterministic or probabilistic form (chapters 17, 18). Part V (graphs) reaches for the heap on every shortest-path call; Part VI (dynamic programming) reaches for the segment / Fenwick trees on every range-query subproblem; the BSTs underpin every ordered-map type in every language standard library you'll ever touch.
